name: Lister Housing Co-operative (Georgian Tenements)
description: These weathered Georgian tenements — built between 1816 and 1824 — are buildings that came within a whisker of being bulldozed for a university campus expansion. By the 1970s they'd fallen into near-slum conditions, and the University of Edinburgh, which owned the block, planned to demolish all 135 flats. The turning point came in 1976, when an eight-year-old girl fell on a nearby building site, an accident that galvanised students, lecturers and long-term working-class residents to join forces and fight the demolition. They won, forming a housing co-operative — Scotland's first co-operative registered social landlord — that renovated the tenements between 1978 and 1982. Today Lister houses almost 400 people across 185 properties.

name: George Heriot's School Turrets
description: Count the corners of the quadrangle and you'll find a turret at each one, but look closer still and notice that no two are quite alike — a deliberate touch of individuality on an otherwise rigidly symmetrical building. These pepper-pot towers, crenellations and castle-like details were meant to impress and even intimidate when the school first rose here from 1628, a statement of wealth from a building fund created by a goldsmith's fortune. Their turreted silhouette has since taken on a life of its own: fans of Harry Potter often point to Heriot's, with its four-house system in Hogwarts-matching colours, as the inspiration for the fictional school — a claim J.K. Rowling herself has denied, insisting Hogwarts was conceived long before she ever saw the building.

name: Ornate Iron Railings
description: Run your eye along the ironwork in front of these tenements and you'll notice the pattern repeats with real precision — swirling finials, evenly spaced verticals, the kind of decorative flourish that Georgian builders added even to something as mundane as a boundary fence. Railings like these once lined nearly every New Town and Georgian street in Edinburgh, but two world wars saw huge numbers melted down for scrap metal, making well-preserved stretches like this one, protected today as part of a listed building, increasingly rare survivors of the city's original streetscape.

name: Iron Boot Scraper
description: Crouch down and you'll find it bolted beside the doorway — a simple iron blade, worn smooth at the edge, set there for one very practical purpose. Before Edinburgh's streets were properly paved, this was where residents scraped the mud, horse dung and grime off their boots before stepping inside. It's a small, easily overlooked survivor of an age when getting from the street to your front door was a genuinely messy business, and a reminder that not every piece of the city's history hangs in a museum.

name: Flower-Decorated Tenement Steps
description: Notice how someone has taken the trouble here — pots crowded onto the stone steps, blooms spilling over the edges, colour against the grey sandstone. It's a small, unofficial act of care, the kind repeated on doorsteps across Edinburgh's tenement streets, where residents quietly claim a few square feet of shared stone as their own. Just a resident deciding that the entrance to their close deserved a bit more life than bare steps alone could offer — a tiny, living rebuttal to the idea that stone stairwells have to stay grey and functional all year round.

name: Argyle House - 60s architectural eyesore
description: Crane your neck up at the sheer grey bulk of this precast concrete tower and you'll understand why Edinburgh residents have argued about it for decades — some see a monstrous carbuncle, others a defiant piece of honest modernism worth protecting. Built in 1968 to designs by Michael Laird & Partners, its ten and eleven storeys of raw concrete stand in stark contrast to the sandstone streets around it, earning it a long-running reputation as the city's biggest eyesore. More recently it found unlikely fame as a filming location for Netflix's Dept Q and the TV adaptation of Irvine Welsh's Crime, before its owners announced plans to demolish it entirely for a mixed-use redevelopment, a move architects and heritage campaigners are still fighting to stop.

name: 6VT Edinburgh City Youth Cafe
description: An unassuming doorway on the Vennel, but step through it and you'll find one of the city centre's few genuinely free social spaces built entirely for young people. 6VT has run as a youth charity here for around two decades, offering a safe drop-in space several nights a week for teenagers and young adults, alongside personal development support, educational workshops and advice services. Over the years its remit has grown well beyond a simple café, extending into housing support and community services for young people facing care or housing instability — a quiet, steady presence in a part of town better known for its castle views than its social services.

name: Brown's Place
description: Picture this small, quiet close two centuries ago: the old city wall crumbling nearby, and an enterprising innkeeper spotting an opportunity. James Brown, who ran an inn in the Grassmarket, owned land backing onto the Vennel, which for centuries had marked the very edge of Edinburgh — the city's boundary here stood until 1856. Once the Flodden Wall was demolished as redundant after the Napoleonic Wars, Brown carved a new square out of his back-lands, likely recycling the wall's own stone into his new houses, and the resulting close still bears his name today, tucked beside the surviving Flodden Tower a little further up the Vennel.

name: Stone Basements and Area Wells
description: A sunken stone pit sits behind iron railings at the foot of the building, a small gulf between pavement and wall. These are area wells, a standard feature of Georgian and Victorian tenement design, dug out to let daylight and fresh air reach the basement level below street height, where servants' quarters, sculleries and coal stores were once tucked away out of sight. It's a detail so ordinary it barely registers, yet it quietly reveals how these buildings were once organised — a below-stairs world working just beneath the feet of everyone walking past above.
